Sample text:
---
# The Museum of Weather

There was a museum in a seaside town that collected weather no longer wanted. Its official name was the Institute of Atmospheric Memory, though everyone called it the Rain Museum, because rain was what visitors understood. They came to see the storm that flooded the old market in 1932, the blizzard that stranded the fishing fleet, the heatwave that made the hills smell of thyme and dust. Each storm occupied a glass room. Visitors pressed their palms to the glass and imagined themselves beneath somebody else’s enormous sky.

I worked there as a night custodian, which meant polishing empty corridors while moonlight moved across the floors. I knew every room by sound. Hailstones clicked in their chamber like applause. Fog whispered behind silver doors. Thunder slept in a copper coil, and when I tested it with a velvet brush, the whole building shivered.

My father founded the museum. Before he became a collector, he was a meteorologist with ink-stained fingers and a habit of standing outdoors during storms as if they were concerts. He believed weather was a language, and every cloud had a sentence to say. “People complain about rain,” he told me, “because they cannot remember being rain themselves. But water has been falling for billions of years. It wants only to arrive.”

When he died, he left me the museum, the keys, and one peculiar instruction: keep the lights on in Room Seven. I never visited that room during the day. Its plaque said only: *Weather of first snow, 14 February 1986*. Yet every night at 2:17 in the morning, I heard footsteps inside. Soft, uneven steps, like those of a child walking through fresh powder.

For seven years I obeyed. I cleaned the other rooms, repaired torn curtains, catalogued donated umbrellas, and pretended not to wonder why the museum had been losing money long before I arrived. The town had changed. Fishers sold their boats to tourists. Children learned the names of screens before stars. On clear nights, the harbor glittered so brightly that nobody looked up.

Then the council announced that the old building would become a hotel. The weather rooms would be sold separately to collectors rich enough to transport them. I was given six months to close the collection.

On the final night, I entered Room Seven. The snow had vanished from its display years ago. The room was bare except for a wooden chair, a small window, and a silver line along the floor. When I stepped over it, the air turned cold. Frost branched across the window. Beyond the glass, though the museum stood three blocks from the sea, I could see a hill buried in white.

A boy stood at the top of the hill, holding a red mitten in one hand and reaching toward the sky with the other. Snowflakes struck his palm and vanished. I knew that gesture. I had seen it in my father’s oldest photograph, taken on the morning of my birth during that famous first snow. He was not in the picture, but the mitten was his, and the hill was behind our childhood house.

Then the room filled with the smell of pine, cold earth, and clean wool. I felt snow melt against my cheeks. For a moment I was seven years old, kneeling in a garden, trying to catch a snowflake because my father had promised that if I caught one whole, I would see where it came from.

“Every snowflake is a place no one has visited,” he had said. “That is why they fall.”

Then, when the vision faded, there was an envelope on the chair. Inside was a note in his handwriting: *You were born in this weather. Take it with you.*

I spent the next morning packing the museum. Most of it could be sold, but Room Seven refused every crate and box. Snow kept appearing in places that had been empty: on the windowsill, across the floor, clinging to my sleeves. So I did what any reasonable curator would do. I dismantled the room piece by piece and carried it into a canvas satchel.

The chair became awkward under my arm. The window I wrapped in blankets. A shovel appeared in a closet and fit perfectly over my shoulder. As I carried these objects toward the coast, the weather followed. Snow settled on the hotel’s roof, silenced traffic, softened voices, and turned the town white enough that all its sharp edges disappeared.

The hotel owners were furious at first, then fascinated. We placed Room Seven on the top floor, facing east. By morning there was a hill outside the window where none had existed. The boy with the red mitten stood there each dawn, but no one else could see him except children and very old people. Children ran down the stairs laughing, announcing that the hill had rabbits, pine trees, and a snowman who changed shape every hour.

I stayed to help run the place. In the evenings, I opened the old weather rooms in the basement: fog, thunder, rain, heat. Guests wandered through them as though they were art galleries. Some laughed. Some stood silent. A woman touched the wall of the 1932 flood and said she could smell wet stone from a town she had never visited. A sailor stood inside the blizzard and wept because it was exactly the snow of his first winter at sea.

Years passed. The hotel became famous, though not for luxury. People came from distant cities to stand in the hill’s impossible morning and wait for the boy to lift his mitten. In winter, no footprint melted until sunrise. In spring, a single pear tree blossomed on the slope, though no one had ever planted it.

I never explained the museum’s disappearance. Museums, I have come to believe, are not about what they keep. They are about what makes people remember. A storm behind glass is merely weather until it touches your skin. A childhood storm, once it finds you again, can open the whole world.

My father was partly wrong. Snowflakes do not fall so anyone can see where they came from; they fall because the world gives itself away. Still, one rests in my palm, bright and intricate, and I wonder where it has been.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A polished magical-realist story builds its emotional turn around a museum that preserves weather and a daughter’s childhood memory.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient, tender, and quietly enchanted, treating weather not as spectacle but as a medium through which memory can return. The narrator’s grief for her father is expressed through sensory details—frost, pine, wool, snow on her cheeks—rather than direct lament. The story invites the reader to let the impossible feel intimate: a remembered storm can become something shared, carried, and encountered again.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds weather as memory and language, the inheritance of a parent’s way of seeing, and the contrast between an attentive childhood imagination and a town distracted by screens and tourism. Its recurring objects—the red mitten, the glass rooms, the snowflake—make preservation feel less like ownership than renewed contact. The moral resolution favors wonder and human connection over commercial conversion, while leaving room for uncertainty about where the snow came from.

## Evidence line
> Museums, I have come to believe, are not about what they keep.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the story is coherent and distinctive, with its weather-and-memory imagery recurring through the plot and shaping its moral resolution.
